items.question: Trace the evolution of the Indian Constitution from the Regulating Act of 1773 to the Government of India Act of 1935. How far did these colonial statutes shape the structure of independent India's Constitution?
items.modelAnswer:
The Indian Constitution did not emerge in a vacuum; its **structural DNA was incubated over 160 years of British legislation**. Under **Company Rule**, the **Regulating Act 1773** took the first step by creating the office of **Governor-General of Bengal** and a Supreme Court at Calcutta, while **Pitt's India Act 1784** introduced the **Board of Control** and the idea of a supervised, accountable executive. The **Charter Act 1833** centralised law-making by creating the **Governor-General of India**, and the **Charter Act 1853** separated legislative from executive functions and opened the civil services to **merit-based competition** — seeds of both a professional bureaucracy and a proto-legislature.

**Crown Rule** deepened these institutions. The **Government of India Act 1858** replaced the Company with direct Crown administration under a **Viceroy** and a **Secretary of State**. The **Indian Councils Acts of 1861, 1892 and 1909** progressively admitted Indians to legislative councils, allowed budget discussion, and — controversially — introduced **separate electorates** (Morley-Minto). The **Act of 1919** experimented with **dyarchy**, and the **Government of India Act 1935** — the 'longest' colonial statute — provided **provincial autonomy, a Federal Court, a distribution of powers through three lists, and an all-India federal scheme**.

The **1935 Act in particular supplied the skeleton** of the 1950 Constitution: the federal structure, office of Governor, emergency-style provisions and the very technique of an exhaustive written document were inherited and refined. Yet the framers made a decisive break — replacing a **colonial, unaccountable order with popular sovereignty, Fundamental Rights and universal adult franchise**. Thus the colonial statutes furnished the **institutional grammar**, but the Constituent Assembly supplied the **democratic vocabulary** that transformed subjects into citizens.
keyPoints: Company Rule: Regulating Act 1773 (GG of Bengal, Supreme Court), Pitt's Act 1784 (Board of Control), Charter Acts 1833 (GG of India) and 1853 (legislative-executive separation, open ICS).
Crown Rule: GoI Act 1858 (Viceroy, Secretary of State); Councils Acts 1861/1892/1909 (Indian inclusion, budget, separate electorates).
GoI Act 1919 introduced dyarchy; GoI Act 1935 gave provincial autonomy, Federal Court and the three-list distribution.
The 1935 Act supplied the structural framework (federalism, Governor, emergency, written form) of the Constitution.
Break from the colonial order: popular sovereignty, Fundamental Rights and universal adult franchise replaced an unaccountable administration.

items.question: Discuss the composition and working of the Constituent Assembly of India. Was it a truly representative body? Critically examine.
items.modelAnswer:
The **Constituent Assembly**, constituted in 1946 under the **Cabinet Mission Plan**, was the crucible in which the Constitution was forged. Its planned strength of **389 seats** (292 from provinces, 93 from princely states, 4 from Chief Commissioners' provinces) fell to **299 after partition**. Members were **indirectly elected** by provincial legislatures through **proportional representation with a single transferable vote**, while princely-state representatives were nominated by their rulers.

Its **working** was methodical and consensual. The first sitting on **9 December 1946** was chaired by the temporary President **Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha**; **Dr. Rajendra Prasad** soon became permanent President, aided by Vice-President **H.C. Mukherjee** and Constitutional Advisor **B.N. Rau**. Nehru's **Objectives Resolution (13 Dec 1946)** set the philosophical compass. Work was distributed among **8 major and 15 minor committees**, the most important being the **Drafting Committee under Dr. B.R. Ambedkar**. Over **11 sessions** spanning **2 years, 11 months and 18 days**, the Assembly debated clause by clause and adopted the Constitution on **26 November 1949**.

On **representativeness**, criticisms are real: it was **indirectly elected, not chosen by universal adult franchise**; it was **Congress-dominated**; and the Muslim League's boycott left it initially incomplete. Yet it was **remarkably inclusive in spirit** — it contained members from every religion, region, and community, and women such as Sarojini Naidu and Durgabai Deshmukh, and its debates gave voice to minorities and the depressed classes. Granville Austin rightly called it a **'one-party dominance' that functioned like a microcosm of the nation**. On balance, though not electorally perfect, the Assembly was **substantively representative** and secured legitimacy through open, deliberative consensus.
keyPoints: Constituted 1946 under the Cabinet Mission Plan; 389 seats reduced to 299 after partition.
Members indirectly elected by provincial assemblies (proportional representation, single transferable vote); princely-state members nominated.
Working: first meeting 9 Dec 1946 (Sinha temporary chair), Rajendra Prasad permanent President, B.N. Rau advisor; Objectives Resolution by Nehru.
8 major + 15 minor committees; Drafting Committee under Ambedkar; 11 sessions over 2y 11m 18d; adopted 26 Nov 1949.
Critique: indirectly elected, Congress-dominated, League boycott — yet inclusive of all communities and women, and consensual in method; substantively representative.
